content.text: What is a Computing Innovation?

A computing innovation is anything that includes a program as an integral part of its function. Innovations are created to solve problems or to pursue interests through creative expression. The key question is: does it require a program to function? If yes, it is a computing innovation.

content.definition: Any innovation that includes a program as an integral part of its function. Can be physical (e.g., self-driving car), nonphysical computing software (e.g., photo editing app), or a nonphysical computing concept (e.g., e-commerce).

rows: Physical
A tangible device that requires a program to function
Self-driving car, smart insulin pump, fitness tracker, smart thermostat
Nonphysical Software
A standalone application or program
Photo editing app, word processor, video game, navigation app
Nonphysical Concept
A system or model that exists because of computing
E-commerce, social media platforms, online banking, ride-sharing services
Smart insulin pump (requires a program to monitor and dose insulin)
A mechanical clock (operates entirely through gears and springs — no program)
Ride-sharing service (requires a program to match drivers and riders)
A printed cookbook (no program required to use it)
Photo editing app (program is integral to the editing function)
A bicycle (no program required to function)

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: The test is always: does the innovation REQUIRE a program as an integral part of its function? A smart car needs a program — it is a computing innovation. A regular car does not need a program to drive — it is not. Don't confuse 'has electronics' with 'requires a program.'
Why Collaboration Matters

Incorporating multiple perspectives through collaboration improves computing innovations as they are developed. When people with different backgrounds, experiences, and viewpoints work together, they catch each other's blind spots, identify needs that a single person might miss, and produce a better final product.

items: Effective collaboration produces a computing innovation that reflects the diversity of talents and perspectives of those who designed it
Collaboration that includes diverse perspectives helps avoid bias in the development of computing innovations
Consultation and communication with users are important aspects of the development of computing innovations
Information gathered from potential users helps understand the purpose of a program from diverse perspectives and develop a program that fully incorporates those perspectives

content.text: How Diversity Prevents Bias: A Real Example

Imagine a team building a voice recognition system that consists entirely of native English speakers from the same region. They test it thoroughly among themselves and it works great — for them. After release, they discover it works poorly for users with accents, non-native speakers, and people with certain speech patterns. The team's lack of diverse perspectives meant they never noticed the system's failure modes for users different from themselves.

content.label: Key Idea
content.text: Bias in computing innovations often happens when the development team is not diverse. If everyone on the team shares the same background, they will likely miss the needs of users who are different from them. This is why diverse perspectives are not just 'nice to have' — they are essential for building fair and effective innovations.
Collaboration vs. Group Work

Effective collaboration is different from simply working in a group. Collaboration requires equal participation and voice from all members. Everyone contributes meaningfully, disagreements are resolved constructively, and the final product reflects the input of the whole team — not just the loudest voice.

rows: All members have equal participation and voice
Some members dominate, others barely contribute
Disagreements are resolved through conflict resolution and negotiation
Disagreements are avoided or ignored
The final product reflects diverse perspectives
The final product reflects only the strongest personality's preferences
Users from diverse backgrounds are consulted
Only team members' own experiences are considered

content.text: How Teams Collaborate: Tools and Models

content.definition: A collaboration model where one programmer writes code while another observes and provides real-time feedback. The observer actively contributes by catching errors the writer might miss. Roles are typically switched regularly.

rows: Writer
Types the code, focuses on implementing the current task
Handles the immediate coding work
Observer
Watches the code being written, points out errors, thinks ahead
Catches mistakes in real time, considers the bigger picture — both roles actively contribute

content.label: Common Mistake
content.text: Students sometimes think the observer in pair programming is not really contributing because they are not writing code. Wrong — the observer actively contributes by catching errors and providing real-time feedback. This is a key benefit of pair programming.

Beyond pair programming, online tools support collaboration by allowing programmers to share and provide feedback on ideas and documents. These tools allow teams to work together across distances, share code, leave comments, track changes, and review each other's contributions asynchronously.

rows: Online code repositories
Allow teams to share, review, and comment on each other's code across locations and time zones
Pair programming
One programmer writes while another observes and gives real-time feedback — both actively contribute
User surveys
Collect structured feedback from many potential users at scale
User interviews
Gather in-depth perspectives from individual users
Direct user observation
Watch how users actually interact with the product to identify problems they may not verbalize
User testing sessions
Let real users try the product and observe where they struggle

content.text: The Four Interpersonal Skills

Effective collaborative teams practice specific interpersonal skills. These are not technical programming skills — they are about how team members interact with each other to make the collaboration productive.

content.definition: Clearly and effectively sharing ideas, progress, concerns, and feedback with all team members so everyone stays informed and aligned.
Working toward an agreement that all team members can accept and support, even if it is not everyone's original preference. The goal is alignment, not just majority rule.
Identifying and addressing disagreements within the team in a productive way that allows the project to move forward without lasting damage to team relationships.
Working through differences in opinion or approach to reach a compromise that satisfies the core needs of the team and the project.

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: You must know exactly four interpersonal skills: communication, consensus building, conflict resolution, and negotiation. These are distinct from collaboration models (like pair programming) and from investigation methods (like surveys). Do not mix these up on the exam.
Gathering User Feedback During Development

Consultation and communication with users are important aspects of the development of computing innovations. Information gathered from potential users can be used to understand the purpose of a program from diverse perspectives and to develop a program that fully incorporates those perspectives.

rows: Surveys
Collecting structured responses from many users via questionnaires
Getting broad input from a large number of users efficiently
Interviews
One-on-one conversations with individual users
Getting in-depth perspectives and follow-up questions
User testing
Watching users interact with the product and observing where they struggle
Identifying usability problems users may not be able to articulate
Direct observation
Watching how users currently perform the task the program will address
Understanding the real problem before designing the solution

content.label: Common Mistake
content.text: A developer's own experience with similar programs is NOT sufficient to understand all user needs. One person's experience represents only one perspective. Gathering input from diverse actual users — especially those who are different from the developers — is essential to building a program that works for everyone.
Summary: What to Know for the Exam

items: A computing innovation must include a program as an integral part of its function — it can be physical, nonphysical software, or a nonphysical concept
Effective collaboration produces innovations that reflect diverse perspectives and helps avoid bias
Collaboration requires equal participation and voice from all members — this is different from just working in a group
Pair programming: one writes, one observes and gives real-time feedback — BOTH actively contribute
Online tools support collaboration by enabling sharing and feedback across distances
The four interpersonal skills: communication, consensus building, conflict resolution, negotiation
Consultation and communication with users are important aspects of development
Information gathered from diverse potential users helps develop a program that fully incorporates those perspectives
Investigation methods include surveys, interviews, user testing, and direct observation
